extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners (and patent practitioners evaluating §101 abstract-idea issues)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a patent claim is directed to an abstract idea (particularly the 'mental processes' and human-activity groupings) under 35 U.S.C. §101, with case law examples and application points for examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting fundamental economic practices—e.g., hedging risk, managing insurance, intermediated settlement, offer-based price optimization—are directed to abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit have characterized hedging and other core economic practices as 'fundamental economic practice' abstract ideas (e.g., Bilski; Alice; Bancorp). Examples listed include: mitigating settlement risk (Alice), rules for conducting a wagering game (In re Smith), financial instruments designed to protect against investment risk (In re Chorna), offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs. v. Amazon), local processing of payments for remotely purchased goods (Inventor Holdings v. Bed Bath Beyond), using an external marking on mail to communicate sender/recipient/contents (Secured Mail Solutions v. Universal Wilde), and placing an order based on displayed market information (Trading Technologies v. IBG).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to commercial interactions or legal interactions—agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales activities, or business relations—are treated as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: buySAFE's transaction performance guaranty (contractual relationship) found abstract; Bancorp's managing a stable-value life insurance policy (calculations supporting a contractual relationship); Fort Properties' tax-advantaged real-estate portfolio tool (legal obligation); Ultramercial's advertising-as-currency scheme (advertising/exchange); Credit Acceptance's processing of financing applications (business relations); Dealertrack's clearing-house processing (business relation). The guideline lists these categories and multiple case examples to show the kinds of commercial/legal interactions that courts have deemed abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing personal behavior or relationships/interactions between people (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that manage personal behavior, social activities, teaching, or following rules/instructions—i.e., methods of organizing human activity or interpersonal interactions—are abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tracking spending/budgeting (Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One), filtering content (BASCOM v. AT&T Mobility), considering historical usage while inputting data (BSG Tech. v. Buyseasons), neurologist mental-process testing steps (In re Meyer), voting/ballot verification (Voter Verified v. ESS), providing information without interfering with primary activity (Interval Licensing v. AOL), and rules for playing games (In re Marco Guldenaar). The guideline emphasizes these are longstanding human activities and thus abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts performed in the human mind—observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions—or processes that can be performed mentally or with simple aids (pen and paper) are abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts consider mental processes that 'can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper' to be abstract ideas (CyberSource; Benson; Mayo; Parker v. Flook). The guideline instructs examiners to treat 'mental processes' as a type of abstract idea applicable to both process and product claims, and provides case law and examples. It warns that mental-process findings apply even when claims are framed as computer-implemented, unless the claim limitations cannot practically be performed by a human.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point A: Claim limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind do not recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If claimed limitations cannot practically be performed by a human (i.e., the human mind is not equipped to perform them), the claim does not fall into the 'mental process' abstract-idea grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should identify whether the limitation requires capabilities beyond human mental performance (e.g., network-packet analysis, GPS pseudorange calculations, specific encryption steps, pixel-by-pixel digital-image halftoning). Cases: SRI Int’l v. Cisco (network monitors/packets), SiRF Tech. (GPS pseudorange calculations), Synopsys (specific encryption/data-manipulation), Research Corp. Techs. (halftoning images). The guideline gives concrete claim examples that were held not to be mental processes because they require non-mental technical operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point B: Claims that encompass a human performing the steps mentally (with or without a physical aid) recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim limitations can practically be performed by a human mentally, even using simple physical aids (pen and paper, slide rule), the limitation falls within the mental-process grouping and is an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The use of a physical aid does not negate the mental nature of a limitation; it merely accounts for human memory/capacity differences. Examples: Benson (mental conversion algorithm), CyberSource (constructing a map of credit card numbers by writing down transactions), Synopsys (translating a functional description to hardware), University of Florida v. GE (analysis described as pen-and-paper flowsheets). Examiners should look to the specification to determine whether claimed steps are essentially performable mentally or with simple aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point C: A claim that requires a computer may still recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting steps performed on a computer can nonetheless be mental-process abstract ideas if the underlying concept can be performed mentally or with pen and paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in view of the specification to see if the applicant is merely claiming a concept performed on a generic computer or using a computer as a tool. The guideline cites Benson and Mortgage Grader as examples where computer-implemented claims were nonetheless abstract because humans could perform the claimed concept. The examiner should review whether the specification describes the concept as being performed in the human mind and only claimed as computer-implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point C.1: Performing a mental process on a generic computer remains an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claims merely recite performing a mental process on a generic computer (i.e., human cognitive actions implemented on general-purpose hardware), the claim can still be directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Voter Verified v. ESS (voting, verifying, and submitting performed on a computer were human cognitive actions and thus abstract); Versata (pricing implemented using general-purpose computer hardware still found to be an abstract idea). Examiners should rely on the specification and claim language to determine whether the computer elements are generic and the claimed invention is essentially a mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental-process applicability to product and process claim types (Point D reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both product (e.g., systems, computer-readable media) and process claims can recite a 'mental process' type abstract idea; the 'mental processes' label refers to the type of abstract idea, not the statutory claim category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts have identified product claims (systems and computer-readable media) as reciting mental-process abstract ideas (e.g., Versata). Examiners should therefore evaluate product claims for mental-process content, not assume only method claims can be mental processes. (The guideline notes this concept and refers examiners to further discussion under point D.)
